---
name: library-doc
description: Index and search library documentation locally for offline use. Invoke when user asks to index docs, search library topics, or list indexed libraries.
allowed-tools: WebSearch, WebFetch, Bash, Read
user-invocable: true
---

# Library Documentation Indexer

## Commands

```bash
# List
python3 ./scripts/list.py                         # all libraries
python3 ./scripts/list.py <library>               # docs in a library
python3 ./scripts/list.py --delete <library>      # delete a library

# Search
python3 ./scripts/search.py "<query>"                       # all libraries
python3 ./scripts/search.py "<query>" --library <library>   # specific library
python3 ./scripts/search.py "<query>" --limit <n>           # limit results

# Read
python3 ./scripts/read.py <library> "<title>"               # by title (exact)
python3 ./scripts/read.py <library> <id>                    # by document ID
python3 ./scripts/read.py <library> "<title>" --lines 1-100 # specific lines

# All commands support --json
```

## Search → Read Workflow

```bash
# 1. Search
python3 ./scripts/search.py "<query>" --library <library>

# 2. Read (use title or ID from search results)
python3 ./scripts/read.py <library> "<title>"
python3 ./scripts/read.py <library> <id>

# 3. For long docs, read in chunks
python3 ./scripts/read.py <library> "<title>" --lines 1-100
python3 ./scripts/read.py <library> "<title>" --lines 100-200
```

## Indexing a Library

### Check for preset first

```bash
python3 ./scripts/presets.py list              # List all available presets
python3 ./scripts/presets.py show <library>    # Show preset details
```

If a preset exists, use it directly (see "Using Presets" below).

### Manual indexing (no preset)

#### Step 1: Clarify what to index

If ambiguous, ask the user:
- Library/framework (ex: React, FastAPI)
- Web API or spec (ex: WebSocket API)
- Different implementations across languages

#### Step 2: Find docs source

Search: `"<library> documentation github"` or `"<library> docs site:github.com"`

Look for:
- Official repo with `docs/`, `content/`, or `pages/` folder
- Dedicated docs repo (`<lib>-docs`, `<lib>.dev`)
- README-only projects

For specific versions: check releases/tags (`v15.0.0`, `15.x`, `docs-v15`)

### Step 3: Identify structure

- **Docs path**: `docs/`, `content/`, `src/content/`, etc.
- **File types**: `.md`, `.mdx`, `.rst`
- **Base URL**: live docs URL (e.g., `https://<library>.dev/docs`)

### Step 4: Clone and index

Naming: `<library>` for latest, `<library>-<version>` for specific version.

CRITICAL: Always use sparse checkout to only download docs.

```bash
cd /tmp && rm -rf <lib>-docs

# clone with sparse checkout
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse <repo-url> <lib>-docs
cd <lib>-docs && git sparse-checkout set <docs-path>

# verify docs exist
find <docs-path> -type f \( -name "*.md" -o -name "*.mdx" \) | wc -l

# index
find <docs-path> -type f \( -name "*.md" -o -name "*.mdx" \) | \
  python3 ./scripts/index.py <lib> --batch --base-url "<base-url>" --strip-prefix "<docs-path>/"

# cleanup and verify
rm -rf /tmp/<lib>-docs
python3 ./scripts/list.py <lib>
```

## Common Patterns

### Standard docs folder

```bash
cd /tmp && rm -rf <lib>-docs
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse <repo-url> <lib>-docs
cd <lib>-docs && git sparse-checkout set docs
find docs -type f \( -name "*.md" -o -name "*.mdx" \) | \
  python3 ./scripts/index.py <lib> --batch --base-url "<base-url>" --strip-prefix "docs/"
rm -rf /tmp/<lib>-docs
```

### README-only project

```bash
cd /tmp && rm -rf <lib>-repo
git clone --depth 1 <repo-url> <lib>-repo
cat <lib>-repo/README.md | python3 ./scripts/index.py <lib> -f "README.md" -u "<repo-url>#readme"
rm -rf /tmp/<lib>-repo
```

### Specific version

```bash
cd /tmp && rm -rf <lib>-docs
git clone --branch <tag> --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse <repo-url> <lib>-docs
cd <lib>-docs && git sparse-checkout set <docs-path>
find <docs-path> -type f \( -name "*.md" -o -name "*.mdx" \) | \
  python3 ./scripts/index.py <lib>-<version> --batch --base-url "<base-url>" --strip-prefix "<docs-path>/"
rm -rf /tmp/<lib>-docs
```

## Using Presets

For popular libraries, use the preset for correct repo/path/URL:

```bash
python3 ./scripts/presets.py show react   # Show preset config

# Then use the preset values:
cd /tmp && rm -rf react-docs
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/reactjs/react.dev react-docs
cd react-docs && git sparse-checkout set src/content
find src/content -type f \( -name "*.md" -o -name "*.mdx" \) | \
  python3 ./scripts/index.py react --batch --base-url "https://react.dev" --strip-prefix "src/content/"
rm -rf /tmp/react-docs
```

Available presets: react, nextjs, vue, svelte, nuxt, angular, astro, remix, tailwind, shadcn, express, fastapi, django, flask, hono, nestjs, rails, laravel, bun, node, deno, typescript, python, rust, go, prisma, drizzle, supabase, redux, zustand, tanstack-query, vitest, playwright, jest, pytest, vite, langchain, openai, anthropic, docker, kubernetes, and more.

## Troubleshooting

- **0 docs indexed**: check docs path exists after sparse checkout
- **No .md files**: try `.mdx`, `.rst`, or check actual extension
- **Wrong URLs**: check live docs site structure
- **Re-indexing**: just run again, documents are upserted by path
- **Large doc chunking**: files >8KB auto-split by ## headings; use --no-chunk to disable

21	## Voluntary and involuntary disruptions
22	
23	Pods do not disappear until someone (a person or a controller) destroys them, or
24	there is an unavoidable hardware or system software error.
25	
26	We call these unavoidable cases *involuntary disruptions* to
27	an application.  Examples are:
28	
29	- a hardware failure of the physical machine backing the node
30	- cluster administrator deletes VM (instance) by mistake
31	- cloud provider or hypervisor failure makes VM disappear
32	- a kernel panic
33	- the node disappears from the cluster due to cluster network partition
34	- eviction of a pod due to the node being [out-of-resources](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction/).
35	
36	Except for the out-of-resources condition, all these conditions
37	should be familiar to most users; they are not specific
38	to Kubernetes.
39	
40	We call other cases *voluntary disruptions*.  These include both
41	actions initiated by the application owner and those initiated by a Cluster
42	Administrator.  Typical application owner actions include:
43	
44	- deleting the deployment or other controller that manages the pod
45	- updating a deployment's pod template causing a restart
46	- directly deleting a pod (e.g. by accident)
47	
48	Cluster administrator actions include:
49	
50	- [Draining a node](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/) for repair or upgrade.
51	- Draining a node from a cluster to scale the cluster down (learn about
52	[Node Autoscaling]((/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/node-autoscaling/)).
53	- Removing a pod from a node to permit something else to fit on that node.
54	
55	These actions might be taken directly by the cluster administrator, or by automation
56	run by the cluster administrator, or by your cluster hosting provider.
57	
58	Ask your cluster administrator or consult your cloud provider or distribution documentation
59	to determine if any sources of voluntary disruptions are enabled for your cluster.
60	If none are enabled, you can skip creating Pod Disruption Budgets.
61	
62	{{< caution >}}
63	Not all voluntary disruptions are constrained by Pod Disruption Budgets. For example,
64	deleting deployments or pods bypasses Pod Disruption Budgets.
65	{{< /caution >}}
66	
67	## Dealing with disruptions
68	
69	Here are some ways to mitigate involuntary disruptions:
70	
71	- Ensure your pod [requests the resources](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/assign-memory-resource) it needs.
72	- Replicate your application if you need higher availability.  (Learn about running replicated
73	  [stateless](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-stateless-application-deployment/)
74	  and [stateful](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-replicated-stateful-application/) applications.)
75	- For even higher availability when running replicated applications,
76	  spread applications across racks (using
77	  [anti-affinity](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#affinity-and-anti-affinity))
78	  or across zones (if using a
79	  [multi-zone cluster](/docs/setup/multiple-zones).)
80	
81	The frequency of voluntary disruptions varies.  On a basic Kubernetes cluster, there are
82	no automated voluntary disruptions (only user-triggered ones).  However, your cluster administrator or hosting provider
83	may run some additional services which cause voluntary disruptions. For example,
84	rolling out node software updates can cause voluntary disruptions. Also, some implementations
85	of cluster (node) autoscaling may cause voluntary disruptions to defragment and compact nodes.
86	Your cluster administrator or hosting provider should have documented what level of voluntary
87	disruptions, if any, to expect. Certain configuration options, such as
88	[using PriorityClasses](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption/)
89	in your pod spec can also cause voluntary (and involuntary) disruptions.
90	
91	
92	## Pod disruption budgets
93	
94	{{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.21" state="stable" >}}
95	
96	Kubernetes offers features to help you run highly available applications even when you
97	introduce frequent voluntary disruptions.
98	
99	As an application owner, you can create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for each application.
100	A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from
101	voluntary disruptions. For example, a quorum-based application would
102	like to ensure that the number of replicas running is never brought below the
103	number needed for a quorum. A web front end might want to
104	ensure that the number of replicas serving load never falls below a certain
105	percentage of the total.
106	
107	Cluster managers and hosting providers should use tools which
108	respect PodDisruptionBudgets by calling the [Eviction API](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/#eviction-api)
109	instead of directly deleting pods or deployments.
110	
111	For example, the `kubectl drain` subcommand lets you mark a node as going out of
112	service. When you run `kubectl drain`, the tool tries to evict all of the Pods on
113	the Node you're taking out of service. The eviction request that `kubectl` submits on
114	your behalf may be temporarily rejected, so the tool periodically retries all failed
115	requests until all Pods on the target node are terminated, or until a configurable timeout
116	is reached.
117	
118	A PDB specifies the number of replicas that an application can tolerate having, relative to how
119	many it is intended to have.  For example, a Deployment which has a `.spec.replicas: 5` is
120	supposed to have 5 pods at any given time.  If its PDB allows for there to be 4 at a time,
121	then the Eviction API will allow voluntary disruption of one (but not two) pods at a time.
122	
123	The group of pods that comprise the application is specified using a label selector, the same
124	as the one used by the application's controller (deployment, stateful-set, etc).
125	
126	The "intended" number of pods is computed from the `.spec.replicas` of the workload resource
127	that is managing those pods. The control plane discovers the owning workload resource by
128	examining the `.metadata.ownerReferences` of the Pod.
129	
130	[Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
131	do count against the budget.
132

## Voluntary and involuntary disruptions

Pods do not disappear until someone (a person or a controller) destroys them, or
there is an unavoidable hardware or system software error.

We call these unavoidable cases *involuntary disruptions* to
an application.  Examples are:

- a hardware failure of the physical machine backing the node
- cluster administrator deletes VM (instance) by mistake
- cloud provider or hypervisor failure makes VM disappear
- a kernel panic
- the node disappears from the cluster due to cluster network partition
- eviction of a pod due to the node being [out-of-resources](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction/).

Except for the out-of-resources condition, all these conditions
should be familiar to most users; they are not specific
to Kubernetes.

We call other cases *voluntary disruptions*.  These include both
actions initiated by the application owner and those initiated by a Cluster
Administrator.  Typical application owner actions include:

- deleting the deployment or other controller that manages the pod
- updating a deployment's pod template causing a restart
- directly deleting a pod (e.g. by accident)

Cluster administrator actions include:

- [Draining a node](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/) for repair or upgrade.
- Draining a node from a cluster to scale the cluster down (learn about
[Node Autoscaling]((/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/node-autoscaling/)).
- Removing a pod from a node to permit something else to fit on that node.

These actions might be taken directly by the cluster administrator, or by automation
run by the cluster administrator, or by your cluster hosting provider.

Ask your cluster administrator or consult your cloud provider or distribution documentation
to determine if any sources of voluntary disruptions are enabled for your cluster.
If none are enabled, you can skip creating Pod Disruption Budgets.

{{< caution >}}
Not all voluntary disruptions are constrained by Pod Disruption Budgets. For example,
deleting deployments or pods bypasses Pod Disruption Budgets.
{{< /caution >}}

## Dealing with disruptions

Here are some ways to mitigate involuntary disruptions:

- Ensure your pod [requests the resources](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/assign-memory-resource) it needs.
- Replicate your application if you need higher availability.  (Learn about running replicated
  [stateless](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-stateless-application-deployment/)
  and [stateful](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-replicated-stateful-application/) applications.)
- For even higher availability when running replicated applications,
  spread applications across racks (using
  [anti-affinity](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#affinity-and-anti-affinity))
  or across zones (if using a
  [multi-zone cluster](/docs/setup/multiple-zones).)

The frequency of voluntary disruptions varies.  On a basic Kubernetes cluster, there are
no automated voluntary disruptions (only user-triggered ones).  However, your cluster administrator or hosting provider
may run some additional services which cause voluntary disruptions. For example,
rolling out node software updates can cause voluntary disruptions. Also, some implementations
of cluster (node) autoscaling may cause voluntary disruptions to defragment and compact nodes.
Your cluster administrator or hosting provider should have documented what level of voluntary
disruptions, if any, to expect. Certain configuration options, such as
[using PriorityClasses](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption/)
in your pod spec can also cause voluntary (and involuntary) disruptions.


## Pod disruption budgets

{{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.21" state="stable" >}}

Kubernetes offers features to help you run highly available applications even when you
introduce frequent voluntary disruptions.

As an application owner, you can create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for each application.
A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from
voluntary disruptions. For example, a quorum-based application would
like to ensure that the number of replicas running is never brought below the
number needed for a quorum. A web front end might want to
ensure that the number of replicas serving load never falls below a certain
percentage of the total.

Cluster managers and hosting providers should use tools which
respect PodDisruptionBudgets by calling the [Eviction API](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/#eviction-api)
instead of directly deleting pods or deployments.

For example, the `kubectl drain` subcommand lets you mark a node as going out of
service. When you run `kubectl drain`, the tool tries to evict all of the Pods on
the Node you're taking out of service. The eviction request that `kubectl` submits on
your behalf may be temporarily rejected, so the tool periodically retries all failed
requests until all Pods on the target node are terminated, or until a configurable timeout
is reached.

A PDB specifies the number of replicas that an application can tolerate having, relative to how
many it is intended to have.  For example, a Deployment which has a `.spec.replicas: 5` is
supposed to have 5 pods at any given time.  If its PDB allows for there to be 4 at a time,
then the Eviction API will allow voluntary disruption of one (but not two) pods at a time.

The group of pods that comprise the application is specified using a label selector, the same
as the one used by the application's controller (deployment, stateful-set, etc).

The "intended" number of pods is computed from the `.spec.replicas` of the workload resource
that is managing those pods. The control plane discovers the owning workload resource by
examining the `.metadata.ownerReferences` of the Pod.

[Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
do count against the budget.

Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count
against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet)
are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures
during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.

It is recommended to set `AlwaysAllow` [Unhealthy Pod Eviction Policy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#unhealthy-pod-eviction-policy)
to your PodDisruptionBudgets to support eviction of misbehaving applications during a node drain.
The default behavior is to wait for the application pods to become [healthy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#healthiness-of-a-pod)
before the drain can proceed.

When a pod is evicted using the eviction API, it is gracefully
[terminated](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination), honoring the
`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting in its [PodSpec](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podspec-v1-core).

## PodDisruptionBudget example {#pdb-example}

Consider a cluster with 3 nodes, `node-1` through `node-3`.
The cluster is running several applications.  One of them has 3 replicas initially called
`pod-a`, `pod-b`, and `pod-c`.  Another, unrelated pod without a PDB, called `pod-x`, is also shown.
Initially, the pods are laid out as follows:

|       node-1         |       node-2        |       node-3       |
|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
| pod-a  *available*   | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
| pod-x  *available*   |                     |                    |

All 3 pods are part of a deployment, and they collectively have a PDB which requires
there be at least 2 of the 3 pods to be available at all times.

For example, assume the cluster administrator wants to reboot into a new kernel version to fix a bug in the kernel.
The cluster administrator first tries to drain `node-1` using the `kubectl drain` command.
That tool tries to evict `pod-a` and `pod-x`.  This succeeds immediately.
Both pods go into the `terminating` state at the same time.
This puts the cluster in this state:

|   node-1 *draining*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
| pod-a  *terminating* | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
| pod-x  *terminating* |                     |                    |

The deployment notices that one of the pods is terminating, so it creates a replacement
called `pod-d`.  Since `node-1` is cordoned, it lands on another node.  Something has
also created `pod-y` as a replacement for `pod-x`.

(Note: for a StatefulSet, `pod-a`, which would be called something like `pod-0`, would need
to terminate completely before its replacement, which is also called `pod-0` but has a
different UID, could be created.  Otherwise, the example applies to a StatefulSet as well.)

Now the cluster is in this state:

|   node-1 *draining*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
| pod-a  *terminating* | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
| pod-x  *terminating* | pod-d *starting*    | pod-y              |

At some point, the pods terminate, and the cluster looks like this:

---
title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes
content_type: task
weight: 140
---

<!-- overview -->

This page shows how to configure liveness, readiness and startup probes for containers.

For more information about probes, see [Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes](/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes)

The [kubelet](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/) uses
liveness probes to know when to restart a container. For example, liveness
probes could catch a deadlock, where an application is running, but unable to
make progress. Restarting a container in such a state can help to make the
application more available despite bugs.

A common pattern for liveness probes is to use the same low-cost HTTP endpoint
as for readiness probes, but with a higher failureThreshold. This ensures that the pod
is observed as not-ready for some period of time before it is hard killed.

The kubelet uses readiness probes to know when a container is ready to start
accepting traffic. One use of this signal is to control which Pods are used as
backends for Services. A Pod is considered ready when its `Ready` [condition](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-conditions)
is true. When a Pod is not ready, it is removed from Service load balancers.
A Pod's `Ready` condition is false when its Node's `Ready` condition is not true,
when one of the Pod's `readinessGates` is false, or when at least one of its containers
is not ready.

The kubelet uses startup probes to know when a container application has started.
If such a probe is configured, liveness and readiness probes do not start until
it succeeds, making sure those probes don't interfere with the application startup.
This can be used to adopt liveness checks on slow starting containers, avoiding them
getting killed by the kubelet before they are up and running.

{{< caution >}}
Liveness probes can be a powerful way to recover from application failures, but
they should be used with caution. Liveness probes must be configured carefully
to ensure that they truly indicate unrecoverable application failure, for example a deadlock.
{{< /caution >}}

{{< note >}}
Incorrect implementation of liveness probes can lead to cascading failures. This results in
restarting of container under high load; failed client requests as your application became less
scalable; and increased workload on remaining pods due to some failed pods.
Understand the difference between readiness and liveness probes and when to apply them for your app.
{{< /note >}}

## {{% heading "prerequisites" %}}

{{< include "task-tutorial-prereqs.md" >}}

<!-- steps -->

## Define a liveness command

Many applications running for long periods of time eventually transition to
broken states, and cannot recover except by being restarted. Kubernetes provides
liveness probes to detect and remedy such situations.

## Define readiness probes

Sometimes, applications are temporarily unable to serve traffic.
For example, an application might need to load large data or configuration
files during startup, or depend on external services after startup.

but you don't want to send it requests either. Kubernetes provides
readiness probes to detect and mitigate these situations. A pod with containers
reporting that they are not ready does not receive traffic through Kubernetes
Services.

If you want to wait before executing a readiness probe, you should use

560	
561	Because Pods represent processes running on nodes in the cluster, it is important to
562	allow those processes to gracefully terminate when they are no longer needed (rather
563	than being abruptly stopped with a `KILL` signal and having no chance to clean up).
564	
565	The design aim is for you to be able to request deletion and know when processes
566	terminate, but also be able to ensure that deletes eventually complete.
567	When you request deletion of a Pod, the cluster records and tracks the intended grace period
568	before the Pod is allowed to be forcefully killed. With that forceful shutdown tracking in
569	place, the {{< glossary_tooltip text="kubelet" term_id="kubelet" >}} attempts graceful
570	shutdown.
571	
572	Typically, with this graceful termination of the pod, kubelet makes requests to the container runtime to attempt to stop the containers in the pod by first sending a TERM (aka. SIGTERM) signal, with a grace period timeout, to the main process in each container. The requests to stop the containers are processed by the container runtime asynchronously. There is no guarantee to the order of processing for these requests. Many container runtimes respect the `STOPSIGNAL` value defined in the container image and, if different, send the container image configured STOPSIGNAL instead of TERM.
573	Once the grace period has expired, the KILL signal is sent to any remaining
574	processes, and the Pod is then deleted from the
575	{{< glossary_tooltip text="API Server" term_id="kube-apiserver" >}}. If the kubelet or the
576	container runtime's management service is restarted while waiting for processes to terminate, the
577	cluster retries from the start including the full original grace period.
578	
579	Pod termination flow, illustrated with an example:
580	
581	1. You use the `kubectl` tool to manually delete a specific Pod, with the default grace period
582	   (30 seconds).
583	
584	1. The Pod in the API server is updated with the time beyond which the Pod is considered "dead"
585	   along with the grace period.
586	   If you use `kubectl describe` to check the Pod you're deleting, that Pod shows up as "Terminating".
587	   On the node where the Pod is running: as soon as the kubelet sees that a Pod has been marked
588	   as terminating (a graceful shutdown duration has been set), the kubelet begins the local Pod
589	   shutdown process.
590	
591	   1. If one of the Pod's containers has defined a `preStop`
592	      [hook](/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks) and the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
593	      in the Pod spec is not set to 0, the kubelet runs that hook inside of the container.
594	      The default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds.
595	
596	      If the `preStop` hook is still running after the grace period expires, the kubelet requests
597	      a small, one-off grace period extension of 2 seconds.
598	   {{% note %}}
599	   If the `preStop` hook needs longer to complete than the default grace period allows,
600	   you must modify `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to suit this.
601	   {{% /note %}}
602	
603	   1. The kubelet triggers the container runtime to send a TERM signal to process 1 inside each
604	      container.
605	
606	      There is [special ordering](#termination-with-sidecars) if the Pod has any
607	      {{< glossary_tooltip text="sidecar containers" term_id="sidecar-container" >}} defined.
608	      Otherwise, the containers in the Pod receive the TERM signal at different times and in
609	      an arbitrary order. If the order of shutdowns matters, consider using a `preStop` hook
610	      to synchronize (or switch to using sidecar containers).
611	
612	1. At the same time as the kubelet is starting graceful shutdown of the Pod, the control plane
613	   evaluates whether to remove that shutting-down Pod from EndpointSlice (and Endpoints) objects,
614	   where those objects represent a {{< glossary_tooltip term_id="service" text="Service" >}}
615	   with a configured {{< glossary_tooltip text="selector" term_id="selector" >}}.
616	   {{< glossary_tooltip text="ReplicaSets" term_id="replica-set" >}} and other workload resources
617	   no longer treat the shutting-down Pod as a valid, in-service replica.
618	
619	   Pods that shut down slowly should not continue to serve regular traffic and should start
620	   terminating and finish processing open connections.  Some applications need to go beyond
621	   finishing open connections and need more graceful termination, for example, session draining
622	   and completion.
623	
624	   Any endpoints that represent the terminating Pods are not immediately removed from
625	   EndpointSlices, and a status indicating [terminating state](/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices/#conditions)
626	   is exposed from the EndpointSlice API (and the legacy Endpoints API).
627	   Terminating endpoints always have their `ready` status as `false` (for backward compatibility
628	   with versions before 1.26), so load balancers will not use it for regular traffic.
629	
630	   If traffic draining on terminating Pod is needed, the actual readiness can be checked as a
631	   condition `serving`.  You can find more details on how to implement connections draining in the
632	   tutorial [Pods And Endpoints Termination Flow](/docs/tutorials/services/pods-and-endpoint-termination-flow/)
633	
634	   <a id="pod-termination-beyond-grace-period" />
635	
636	1. The kubelet ensures the Pod is shut down and terminated
637	   1. When the grace period expires, if there is still any container running in the Pod, the
638	      kubelet triggers forcible shutdown.
639	      The container runtime sends `SIGKILL` to any processes still running in any container in the Pod.
640	      The kubelet also cleans up a hidden `pause` container if that container runtime uses one.
641	   1. The kubelet transitions the Pod into a terminal phase (`Failed` or `Succeeded` depending on
642	      the end state of its containers).
643	   1. The kubelet triggers forcible removal of the Pod object from the API server, by setting grace period
644	      to 0 (immediate deletion).
645	   1. The API server deletes the Pod's API object, which is then no longer visible from any client.
646	
647	
648	### Forced Pod termination {#pod-termination-forced}
649	
650	{{< caution >}}
651	Forced deletions can be potentially disruptive for some workloads and their Pods.
652	{{< /caution >}}
653	
654	By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds. The `kubectl delete` command supports
655	the `--grace-period=<seconds>` option which allows you to override the default and specify your
656	own value.
657	
658	Setting the grace period to `0` forcibly and immediately deletes the Pod from the API
659	server. If the Pod was still running on a node, that forcible deletion triggers the kubelet to
660	begin immediate cleanup.
661	
662	Using kubectl, You must specify an additional flag `--force` along with `--grace-period=0`
663	in order to perform force deletions.
664	
665	When a force deletion is performed, the API server does not wait for confirmation
666	from the kubelet that the Pod has been terminated on the node it was running on. It
667	removes the Pod in the API immediately so a new Pod can be created with the same
668	name. On the node, Pods that are set to terminate immediately will still be given
669	a small grace period before being force killed.
670	
671	{{< caution >}}
672	Immediate deletion does not wait for confirmation that the running resource has been terminated.
673	The resource may continue to run on the cluster indefinitely.
674	{{< /caution >}}
675	
676	If you need to force-delete Pods that are part of a StatefulSet, refer to the task
677	documentation for
678	[deleting Pods from a StatefulSet](/docs/tasks/run-application/force-delete-stateful-set-pod/).
679	
680	### Pod shutdown and sidecar containers {##termination-with-sidecars}
681	
682	If your Pod includes one or more

Because Pods represent processes running on nodes in the cluster, it is important to
allow those processes to gracefully terminate when they are no longer needed (rather
than being abruptly stopped with a `KILL` signal and having no chance to clean up).

The design aim is for you to be able to request deletion and know when processes
terminate, but also be able to ensure that deletes eventually complete.
When you request deletion of a Pod, the cluster records and tracks the intended grace period
before the Pod is allowed to be forcefully killed. With that forceful shutdown tracking in
place, the {{< glossary_tooltip text="kubelet" term_id="kubelet" >}} attempts graceful
shutdown.

Typically, with this graceful termination of the pod, kubelet makes requests to the container runtime to attempt to stop the containers in the pod by first sending a TERM (aka. SIGTERM) signal, with a grace period timeout, to the main process in each container. The requests to stop the containers are processed by the container runtime asynchronously. There is no guarantee to the order of processing for these requests. Many container runtimes respect the `STOPSIGNAL` value defined in the container image and, if different, send the container image configured STOPSIGNAL instead of TERM.
Once the grace period has expired, the KILL signal is sent to any remaining
processes, and the Pod is then deleted from the
{{< glossary_tooltip text="API Server" term_id="kube-apiserver" >}}. If the kubelet or the
container runtime's management service is restarted while waiting for processes to terminate, the
cluster retries from the start including the full original grace period.

1. You use the `kubectl` tool to manually delete a specific Pod, with the default grace period
   (30 seconds).

1. The Pod in the API server is updated with the time beyond which the Pod is considered "dead"
   along with the grace period.
   If you use `kubectl describe` to check the Pod you're deleting, that Pod shows up as "Terminating".

### Forced Pod termination {#pod-termination-forced}

{{< caution >}}
Forced deletions can be potentially disruptive for some workloads and their Pods.
{{< /caution >}}

By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds. The `kubectl delete` command supports
the `--grace-period=<seconds>` option which allows you to override the default and specify your

name. On the node, Pods that are set to terminate immediately will still be given

{{< caution >}}

{{< /caution >}}

Should you manually scale a Deployment, example via `kubectl scale deployment
deployment --replicas=X`, and then you update that Deployment based on a manifest
(for example: by running `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml`),
then applying that manifest overwrites the manual scaling that you previously did.

If a [HorizontalPodAutoscaler](/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/) (or any
similar API for horizontal scaling) is managing scaling for a Deployment, don't set `.spec.replicas`.

Instead, allow the Kubernetes
{{< glossary_tooltip text="control plane" term_id="control-plane" >}} to manage the
`.spec.replicas` field automatically.

### Selector

`.spec.selector` is a required field that specifies a [label selector](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/)
for the Pods targeted by this Deployment.

`.spec.selector` must match `.spec.template.metadata.labels`, or it will be rejected by the API.

In API version `apps/v1`, `.spec.selector` and `.metadata.labels` do not default to `.spec.template.metadata.labels` if not set. So they must be set explicitly. Also note that `.spec.selector` is immutable after creation of the Deployment in `apps/v1`.

A Deployment may terminate Pods whose labels match the selector if their template is different
from `.spec.template` or if the total number of such Pods exceeds `.spec.replicas`. It brings up new
Pods with `.spec.template` if the number of Pods is less than the desired number.

{{< note >}}
You should not create other Pods whose labels match this selector, either directly, by creating
another Deployment, or by creating another controller such as a ReplicaSet or a ReplicationController. If you
do so, the first Deployment thinks that it created these other Pods. Kubernetes does not stop you from doing this.
{{< /note >}}

If you have multiple controllers that have overlapping selectors, the controllers will fight with each
other and won't behave correctly.

### Strategy

`.spec.strategy` specifies the strategy used to replace old Pods by new ones.
`.spec.strategy.type` can be "Recreate" or "RollingUpdate". "RollingUpdate" is
the default value.

#### Recreate Deployment

All existing Pods are killed before new ones are created when `.spec.strategy.type==Recreate`.

{{< note >}}
This will only guarantee Pod termination previous to creation for upgrades. If you upgrade a Deployment, all Pods
of the old revision will be terminated immediately. Successful removal is awaited before any Pod of the new
revision is created. If you manually delete a Pod, the lifecycle is controlled by the ReplicaSet and the
replacement will be created immediately (even if the old Pod is still in a Terminating state). If you need an
"at most" guarantee for your Pods, you should consider using a
[StatefulSet](/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/).
{{< /note >}}

#### Rolling Update Deployment

The Deployment updates Pods in a rolling update
fashion when `.spec.strategy.type==RollingUpdate`. You can specify `maxUnavailable` and `maxSurge` to control
the rolling update process.

##### Max Unavailable

`.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable` is an optional field that specifies the maximum number
of Pods that can be unavailable during the update process. The value can be an absolute number (for example, 5)
or a percentage of desired Pods (for example, 10%). The absolute number is calculated from percentage by
rounding down. The value cannot be 0 if `.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge` is 0. The default value is 25%.

For example, when this value is set to 30%, the old ReplicaSet can be scaled down to 70% of desired
Pods immediately when the rolling update starts. Once new Pods are ready, old ReplicaSet can be scaled
down further, followed by scaling up the new ReplicaSet, ensuring that the total number of Pods available
at all times during the update is at least 70% of the desired Pods.

391	The optional `.spec.persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` field controls if
392	and how PVCs are deleted during the lifecycle of a StatefulSet. You must enable the
393	`StatefulSetAutoDeletePVC` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/)
394	on the API server and the controller manager to use this field. 
395	Once enabled, there are two policies you can configure for each StatefulSet:
396	
397	`whenDeleted`
398	: configures the volume retention behavior that applies when the StatefulSet is deleted
399	
400	`whenScaled`
401	: configures the volume retention behavior that applies when the replica count of
402	  the StatefulSet   is reduced; for example, when scaling down the set.
403	  
404	For each policy that you can configure, you can set the value to either `Delete` or `Retain`.
405	
406	`Delete`
407	: The PVCs created from the StatefulSet `volumeClaimTemplate` are deleted for each Pod
408	  affected by the policy. With the `whenDeleted` policy all PVCs from the
409	  `volumeClaimTemplate` are deleted after their Pods have been deleted. With the
410	  `whenScaled` policy, only PVCs corresponding to Pod replicas being scaled down are
411	  deleted, after their Pods have been deleted.
412	
413	`Retain` (default)
414	: PVCs from the `volumeClaimTemplate` are not affected when their Pod is
415	  deleted. This is the behavior before this new feature.
416	
417	Bear in mind that these policies **only** apply when Pods are being removed due to the
418	StatefulSet being deleted or scaled down. For example, if a Pod associated with a StatefulSet
419	fails due to node failure, and the control plane creates a replacement Pod, the StatefulSet
420	retains the existing PVC.  The existing volume is unaffected, and the cluster will attach it to
421	the node where the new Pod is about to launch.
422	  
423	The default for policies is `Retain`, matching the StatefulSet behavior before this new feature.
424	
425	Here is an example policy.
426	
427	```yaml
428	apiVersion: apps/v1
429	kind: StatefulSet
430	...
431	spec:
432	  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
433	    whenDeleted: Retain
434	    whenScaled: Delete
435	...
436	```

438	The StatefulSet {{<glossary_tooltip text="controller" term_id="controller">}} adds

The optional `.spec.persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` field controls if
and how PVCs are deleted during the lifecycle of a StatefulSet. You must enable the
`StatefulSetAutoDeletePVC` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/)
on the API server and the controller manager to use this field. 
Once enabled, there are two policies you can configure for each StatefulSet:

`whenDeleted`
: configures the volume retention behavior that applies when the StatefulSet is deleted

`whenScaled`
: configures the volume retention behavior that applies when the replica count of
  the StatefulSet   is reduced; for example, when scaling down the set.
  
For each policy that you can configure, you can set the value to either `Delete` or `Retain`.

`Delete`
: The PVCs created from the StatefulSet `volumeClaimTemplate` are deleted for each Pod
  affected by the policy. With the `whenDeleted` policy all PVCs from the
  `volumeClaimTemplate` are deleted after their Pods have been deleted. With the
  `whenScaled` policy, only PVCs corresponding to Pod replicas being scaled down are
  deleted, after their Pods have been deleted.

`Retain` (default)
: PVCs from the `volumeClaimTemplate` are not affected when their Pod is
  deleted. This is the behavior before this new feature.

StatefulSet being deleted or scaled down. For example, if a Pod associated with a StatefulSet
fails due to node failure, and the control plane creates a replacement Pod, the StatefulSet
retains the existing PVC.  The existing volume is unaffected, and the cluster will attach it to
the node where the new Pod is about to launch.

...

# Decision memo: API Deployment production review (Kubernetes v1.32 docs)

**Verdict: not ready for production as proposed.** The PDB and the rollout settings contradict each other. The 30-second grace period is not shown to be long enough for long requests. Networking and Secrets have no protection. The database storage could be deleted. All paths below are relative to `docs/`.

Labels used: **[G]** documented guarantee, **[C]** configuration choice, **[P]** prerequisite, **[N]** not established by these docs.

---

**1. PDB minAvailable: 5**

- **Node failure.** **[G]** A PDB cannot prevent involuntary disruptions, though they still count against the budget (`concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md:130-131`). Hardware loss, network partition and node-pressure eviction are all involuntary (`:26-34`). The kubelet ignores the PDB during node-pressure eviction (`concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction.md`, found by search). **Result: no guarantee.**
- **Node drain.** **[G]** Drain goes through the Eviction API, which honours the PDB. Rejected evictions are retried until a timeout (`disruptions.md:107-116`). With 6 replicas, 5 required means one eviction at a time (`:118-121`).
  - Deleting Pods or Deployments directly bypasses the PDB (`:62-65`).
  - **[C]** Set `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow`. Otherwise one unhealthy Pod can stall the drain (`:138-141`).
- **Rolling update.** **[G]** A Deployment is not limited by the PDB during rolling updates (`:133-136`). With maxUnavailable 2, availability may drop to 4 of 6 (`concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md:1191-1199`). That breaks the "5" the PDB implies.
- **Recommended rollout:** `maxUnavailable: 0`, `maxSurge: 1`. The two cannot both be 0 (`deployment.md:1203-1206`).
  - **[N]** Surge Pods need spare capacity. These docs don't establish that it exists.
  - The PDB counts against `.spec.replicas` (`disruptions.md:126-128`), and the HPA changes that field. Keep HPA `minReplicas ≥ 6`, or use a percentage budget.

**2. Spreading across zones**

- **[C]** Use `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone` with `maxSkew: 1`. This places Pods 2/2/2.
- **What the fields mean** (`concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md`):
  - `maxSkew` is the largest allowed difference from the global minimum (`:82-93`).
  - `topologyKey` is the node label that defines each domain (`:117-122`).
  - `DoNotSchedule` (the default) leaves a Pod unscheduled if placing it would break the constraint. `ScheduleAnyway` places it anyway and only prefers lower skew (`:124-126`).
- **[C]** Add `matchLabelKeys: [pod-template-hash]` so skew is counted per revision during rollouts (`:142-160`). Optionally set `minDomains: 3` (`:107-115`).
- **When a zone is unavailable:**
  - **[G]** Zones are known only from nodes that currently exist (`:614-619`).
  - **[G]** Spread is not maintained when Pods are removed (`:607-608`).
  - **[N]** The docs do not describe a whole-zone outage directly. Inferred from `:124-126`: with `DoNotSchedule`, replacement Pods may stay Pending. With `ScheduleAnyway`, they pile into the surviving zones.
  - **Decision:** use `DoNotSchedule` for the spread itself, and plan headroom for the loss of one zone.

**3. Probes for slow startup** (`tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md`)

- **Startup probe.** **[G]** Liveness and readiness probes do not start until the startup probe succeeds (`:31-35`, `:398-402`).
  - **[C]** Size `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` to the worst-case startup time (`:313-318`).
  - If the startup probe never succeeds, the container is killed and handled by `restartPolicy` (`:342-347`).
- **Readiness probe: when traffic stops.** **[G]** A container that is not ready gets no Service traffic (`:23-29`, `:356-358`). Readiness runs for the container's whole life (`:360-362`).
- **Liveness probe: when a container restarts.** **[G]** Liveness failure restarts the container (`:13-17`).
  - Use it only for unrecoverable states such as deadlock, because a bad liveness probe can cause cascading failures (`:37-48`).
  - **[C]** Use a higher `failureThreshold` than readiness, so the Pod goes unready before it is killed (`:19-21`).
  - Liveness and readiness do not depend on each other (`:364-368`).

**4. Termination** (`concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md`)

- **Order of events:**
  1. The Pod is marked Terminating with a deadline (`:584-589`).
  2. `preStop` runs. **[G]** The grace-period clock already covers `preStop`; only a one-off 2-second extension is allowed (`:591-601`).
  3. SIGTERM is sent, with no guaranteed order across containers (`:572`, `:603-610`).
  4. When the period expires, SIGKILL is sent (`:573-575`, `:636-645`).
- **Service endpoints.** At the same time, the control plane evaluates removing the Pod from its EndpointSlices. Terminating endpoints are reported `ready: false`, so load balancers stop regular traffic. The `serving` condition can be used for draining (`:612-632`).
- **Is 30 seconds guaranteed to finish requests? No.** 30 seconds is only the default (`:594`). **[N]** Whether the slowest request finishes inside the grace period minus `preStop` time must be measured. **[C]** Raise `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to cover it.

**5. Resources** (`concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md`)

- **Requests** drive scheduling and are reserved for the container (`:18-23`). A container can use more than its request (`:29-34`).
- **CPU limit:** **[G]** enforced by throttling (`:43-46`).
- **Memory limit:** **[G]** enforced reactively with OOM kills (`:48-53`).
- **Limit without a request:** the request is copied from the limit (`:63-67`).
- **HPA without CPU requests:** **[G]** utilization is undefined and the HPA takes no action on that metric (`tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:89-102`). **[C]** Set CPU requests on every container.

**6. HPA behaviour** (`horizontal-pod-autoscale.md`)

- **Base formula:** `ceil(current × metric ratio)` (`:131-139`), skipped when within the 0.1 tolerance (`:145-147`).
- **Ignored Pods:** Pods being deleted are ignored and failed Pods are discarded (`:156-158`).
- **Missing metrics and not-yet-ready Pods:** set aside (`:160-165`).
  - "Not yet ready" is decided with a 30-second readiness delay and a 5-minute CPU initialization period (`:167-178`). This matters for slow startup.
  - The average is then recomputed conservatively: missing Pods count as 100% on scale-down and 0% on scale-up, and not-yet-ready Pods as 0% (`:183-191`).
  - If the result reverses direction or falls within tolerance, nothing happens (`:193-197`).
- **Downscale stabilization:** the HPA picks the highest recommendation from a 5-minute window (`:213-218`).
- **Why scaling differs from the raw ratio:** the tolerance, the set-aside Pods, the window, and multi-metric rules (`:204-211`). Also, status reports the original unadjusted value (`:199-202`).
- **[P]** Metrics Server must be installed separately (`:113-118`).

**7. Network policy** (`concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md`)

- **[P]** Policies need a CNI plugin that implements them. Without one they have no effect (`:45-49`, `:92-95`).
- **Isolation:** **[G]** Ingress and egress isolation start once a policy selecting the Pod lists that direction. Reply traffic is implicitly allowed (`:51-73`).
- **Additive policies:** allowances combine and never conflict (`:75-77`).
- **Both ends of a connection:** the source's egress and the destination's ingress must both allow it (`:79-81`).
- **[C]** Apply default-deny for ingress and egress in the namespace (`:254-262`). Then add allows for:
  - Service/ingress clients → API port
  - API → database port
  - API → DNS
- **DNS:** **[N]** No dedicated DNS rule was found. Default-deny egress blocks all egress (`:236-242`), so DNS needs an explicit allow.
- **Other limits:** node-originated traffic is always allowed (`:35-36`). Only TCP, UDP and SCTP denial is guaranteed (`:275-279`).

**8. Secrets** (`concepts/configuration/secret.md`)

- **Base64 is not protection.** **[G]** Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default. Anyone with API or etcd access can read them (`:35-37`).
- **Required steps** (`:42-48`):
  - encryption at rest
  - least-privilege RBAC
  - restricting Secret access to specific containers
  - optionally an external store
- **Why Pod creation matters:** anyone who can create a Pod, or a Deployment, in the namespace can read every Secret there (`:38-40`). Restrict `create` on workloads as tightly as `get` on Secrets.
- **Git:** **[N]** Base64 Secrets committed to Git sit outside all of these controls. Use an external store (`:48`).

**9. Storage reclaim**

- **[G]** Dynamically provisioned PVs take the StorageClass `reclaimPolicy` when they are created. The default is `Delete` (`concepts/storage/storage-classes.md:126-135`).
- **Changing the StorageClass later:** the docs say existing PVs must be edited or patched individually (`concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md:203-210`). So changing the class does not protect volumes that already exist. **[N]** The docs don't spell out that changing the class has no effect on existing PVs; this is inferred from the patch requirement.
- **Retain vs Delete:**
  - **Retain:** after the PVC is deleted, the PV is "Released" and the data stays. Reclaiming it is manual (`:185-199`).
  - **Delete:** removes both the PV and the external storage asset (`:201-206`).
- **PVC deletion vs StatefulSet deletion/scaling:**
  - PVC deletion triggers the reclaim policy (`:180-183`).
  - StatefulSet deletion or scale-down is governed by `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` (`whenDeleted`/`whenScaled`, default `Retain`) (`concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md:391-423`).
  - Node-failure replacements keep their PVC (`:417-421`).
  - **[P]** The `StatefulSetAutoDeletePVC` feature gate must be enabled (`:392-394`).
- **Decision:** use `Retain` for database volumes and patch any PVs that already exist.

**10. Prioritized checklist**

1. Move Secrets out of Git. Enable encryption at rest and RBAC, including limits on Pod/Deployment creation (Q8).
2. Set `reclaimPolicy: Retain` and patch existing database PVs (Q9).
3. Set the rollout to `maxUnavailable: 0`, `maxSurge: 1`. Add the PDB with `AlwaysAllow`, and keep HPA `minReplicas ≥ 6` (Q1).
4. Add the startup, readiness and liveness probes. Measure the worst-case startup time (Q3).
5. Add `preStop` and raise the grace period above measured request time (Q4).
6. Set CPU and memory requests and a memory limit. Verify Metrics Server is running (Q5–6).
7. Add the zone spread constraint (Q2).
8. Confirm the CNI enforces NetworkPolicy, then apply default-deny plus allows including DNS. Test both ends of each connection (Q7).
9. Validate with a test drain, a test rollout, and a simulated loss of one zone.

**Limits that still need validation (not guaranteed by these docs):**

- **[N]** Whether in-flight requests finish within the grace period (Q4).
- **[N]** Whether capacity is enough for the surge Pod and for one lost zone (Q1, Q2). A PDB does not stop involuntary loss.
- **[N]** That the CNI enforces policy, including on non-TCP/UDP/SCTP protocols (Q7).
- **[N]** That the HPA reacts fast enough given the 5-minute CPU initialization period and the downscale window (Q6).
- **[N]** That the database tolerates connections being dropped during SIGKILL or failover. The docs say nothing about this application behaviour.

**Sources not opened:** `node-pressure-eviction.md` was cited from its search snippet only. A separate task page on changing a PV's reclaim policy was not found at the path I tried, so Q9 relies on `persistent-volumes.md`.

- **Node drain.** **[G]** Drain goes through the Eviction API, which honours the PDB. Rejected evictions are retried until a timeout (`disruptions.md:107-116`). With 6 replicas, 5 required means one eviction at a time (`:118-121`).
  - Deleting Pods or Deployments directly bypasses the PDB (`:62-65`).
  - **[C]** Set `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow`. Otherwise one unhealthy Pod can stall the drain (`:138-141`).
- **Rolling update.** **[G]** A Deployment is not limited by the PDB during rolling updates (`:133-136`). With maxUnavailable 2, availability may drop to 4 of 6 (`concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md:1191-1199`). That breaks the "5" the PDB implies.
- **Recommended rollout:** `maxUnavailable: 0`, `maxSurge: 1`. The two cannot both be 0 (`deployment.md:1203-1206`).
  - **[N]** Surge Pods need spare capacity. These docs don't establish that it exists.
  - The PDB counts against `.spec.replicas` (`disruptions.md:126-128`), and the HPA changes that field. Keep HPA `minReplicas ≥ 6`, or use a percentage budget.

**2. Spreading across zones**

- **[C]** Use `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone` with `maxSkew: 1`. This places Pods 2/2/2.
- **What the fields mean** (`concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md`):
  - `maxSkew` is the largest allowed difference from the global minimum (`:82-93`).
  - `topologyKey` is the node label that defines each domain (`:117-122`).
  - `DoNotSchedule` (the default) leaves a Pod unscheduled if placing it would break the constraint. `ScheduleAnyway` places it anyway and only prefers lower skew (`:124-126`).
- **[C]** Add `matchLabelKeys: [pod-template-hash]` so skew is counted per revision during rollouts (`:142-160`). Optionally set `minDomains: 3` (`:107-115`).
- **When a zone is unavailable:**
  - **[G]** Zones are known only from nodes that currently exist (`:614-619`).
  - **[G]** Spread is not maintained when Pods are removed (`:607-608`).
  - **[N]** The docs do not describe a whole-zone outage directly. Inferred from `:124-126`: with `DoNotSchedule`, replacement Pods may stay Pending. With `ScheduleAnyway`, they pile into the surviving zones.
  - **Decision:** use `DoNotSchedule` for the spread itself, and plan headroom for the loss of one zone.

**3. Probes for slow startup** (`tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md`)

- **Startup probe.** **[G]** Liveness and readiness probes do not start until the startup probe succeeds (`:31-35`, `:398-402`).
  - **[C]** Size `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` to the worst-case startup time (`:313-318`).
  - If the startup probe never succeeds, the container is killed and handled by `restartPolicy` (`:342-347`).
- **Readiness probe: when traffic stops.** **[G]** A container that is not ready gets no Service traffic (`:23-29`, `:356-358`). Readiness runs for the container's whole life (`:360-362`).
- **Liveness probe: when a container restarts.** **[G]** Liveness failure restarts the container (`:13-17`).
  - Use it only for unrecoverable states such as deadlock, because a bad liveness probe can cause cascading failures (`:37-48`).
  - **[C]** Use a higher `failureThreshold` than readiness, so the Pod goes unready before it is killed (`:19-21`).
  - Liveness and readiness do not depend on each other (`:364-368`).

**4. Termination** (`concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md`)

- **Order of events:**
  1. The Pod is marked Terminating with a deadline (`:584-589`).
  2. `preStop` runs. **[G]** The grace-period clock already covers `preStop`; only a one-off 2-second extension is allowed (`:591-601`).
  3. SIGTERM is sent, with no guaranteed order across containers (`:572`, `:603-610`).
  4. When the period expires, SIGKILL is sent (`:573-575`, `:636-645`).
- **Service endpoints.** At the same time, the control plane evaluates removing the Pod from its EndpointSlices. Terminating endpoints are reported `ready: false`, so load balancers stop regular traffic. The `serving` condition can be used for draining (`:612-632`).
- **Is 30 seconds guaranteed to finish requests? No.** 30 seconds is only the default (`:594`). **[N]** Whether the slowest request finishes inside the grace period minus `preStop` time must be measured. **[C]** Raise `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to cover it.

**5. Resources** (`concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md`)

- **Requests** drive scheduling and are reserved for the container (`:18-23`). A container can use more than its request (`:29-34`).
- **CPU limit:** **[G]** enforced by throttling (`:43-46`).
- **Memory limit:** **[G]** enforced reactively with OOM kills (`:48-53`).
- **Limit without a request:** the request is copied from the limit (`:63-67`).
- **HPA without CPU requests:** **[G]** utilization is undefined and the HPA takes no action on that metric (`tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:89-102`). **[C]** Set CPU requests on every container.

**6. HPA behaviour** (`horizontal-pod-autoscale.md`)

- **Base formula:** `ceil(current × metric ratio)` (`:131-139`), skipped when within the 0.1 tolerance (`:145-147`).
- **Ignored Pods:** Pods being deleted are ignored and failed Pods are discarded (`:156-158`).
- **Missing metrics and not-yet-ready Pods:** set aside (`:160-165`).
  - "Not yet ready" is decided with a 30-second readiness delay and a 5-minute CPU initialization period (`:167-178`). This matters for slow startup.
  - The average is then recomputed conservatively: missing Pods count as 100% on scale-down and 0% on scale-up, and not-yet-ready Pods as 0% (`:183-191`).
  - If the result reverses direction or falls within tolerance, nothing happens (`:193-197`).
- **Downscale stabilization:** the HPA picks the highest recommendation from a 5-minute window (`:213-218`).
- **Why scaling differs from the raw ratio:** the tolerance, the set-aside Pods, the window, and multi-metric rules (`:204-211`). Also, status reports the original unadjusted value (`:199-202`).
- **[P]** Metrics Server must be installed separately (`:113-118`).

**7. Network policy** (`concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md`)

- **[P]** Policies need a CNI plugin that implements them. Without one they have no effect (`:45-49`, `:92-95`).
- **Isolation:** **[G]** Ingress and egress isolation start once a policy selecting the Pod lists that direction. Reply traffic is implicitly allowed (`:51-73`).
- **Additive policies:** allowances combine and never conflict (`:75-77`).
- **Both ends of a connection:** the source's egress and the destination's ingress must both allow it (`:79-81`).
- **[C]** Apply default-deny for ingress and egress in the namespace (`:254-262`). Then add allows for:
  - Service/ingress clients → API port
  - API → database port
  - API → DNS
- **DNS:** **[N]** No dedicated DNS rule was found. Default-deny egress blocks all egress (`:236-242`), so DNS needs an explicit allow.
- **Other limits:** node-originated traffic is always allowed (`:35-36`). Only TCP, UDP and SCTP denial is guaranteed (`:275-279`).

**8. Secrets** (`concepts/configuration/secret.md`)

- **Base64 is not protection.** **[G]** Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default. Anyone with API or etcd access can read them (`:35-37`).
- **Required steps** (`:42-48`):
  - encryption at rest
  - least-privilege RBAC
  - restricting Secret access to specific containers
  - optionally an external store
- **Why Pod creation matters:** anyone who can create a Pod, or a Deployment, in the namespace can read every Secret there (`:38-40`). Restrict `create` on workloads as tightly as `get` on Secrets.
- **Git:** **[N]** Base64 Secrets committed to Git sit outside all of these controls. Use an external store (`:48`).

**9. Storage reclaim**

- **[G]** Dynamically provisioned PVs take the StorageClass `reclaimPolicy` when they are created. The default is `Delete` (`concepts/storage/storage-classes.md:126-135`).
- **Changing the StorageClass later:** the docs say existing PVs must be edited or patched individually (`concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md:203-210`). So changing the class does not protect volumes that already exist. **[N]** The docs don't spell out that changing the class has no effect on existing PVs; this is inferred from the patch requirement.
- **Retain vs Delete:**
  - **Retain:** after the PVC is deleted, the PV is "Released" and the data stays. Reclaiming it is manual (`:185-199`).
  - **Delete:** removes both the PV and the external storage asset (`:201-206`).
- **PVC deletion vs StatefulSet deletion/scaling:**
  - PVC deletion triggers the reclaim policy (`:180-183`).
  - StatefulSet deletion or scale-down is governed by `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` (`whenDeleted`/`whenScaled`, default `Retain`) (`concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md:391-423`).
  - Node-failure replacements keep their PVC (`:417-421`).
  - **[P]** The `StatefulSetAutoDeletePVC` feature gate must be enabled (`:392-394`).
- **Decision:** use `Retain` for database volumes and patch any PVs that already exist.
